blocks.text: When the Nigeria Labour Congress calls a nationwide strike over fuel prices, petrol stations close and Lagos traffic thins — yet no NLC candidate appears on any ballot. The union is not trying to become the government. It is trying to make the government change its mind. That is the work of a pressure group.

blocks.title: Pressure group
blocks.text: An organised association that seeks to influence government policy and public opinion in favour of a shared interest or cause, without itself seeking to form or capture government. It applies pressure from outside the formal party contest.

blocks.markdown:
### Types of pressure group

Examiners expect two overlapping classifications.

**By purpose.** An **interest** (or sectional) group exists to defend the material interests of its own members: wages, professional standards, profits. A **promotional** (or cause) group exists to advance a cause that is not confined to its members: environmental protection, human rights, a ban on child marriage.

**By origin and organisation** (Almond's classification, often set in JAMB):
- **Associational** — formally organised, with officials and a constitution: NLC, NBA, NMA.
- **Institutional** — groups that arise inside formal institutions, such as the military, the civil service or a university senate, and press their views from that base.
- **Non-associational** — informal, kinship or ethnic groupings without a standing organisation.
- **Anomic** — spontaneous, poorly organised outbursts such as a riot or a sudden protest, with little lasting structure.

rows: Organised workers' wages, conditions and job security
Doctors' welfare, conditions of service and standards of practice
Lawyers' professional interests and the independence of the legal profession
Industrialists' costs, tariffs, power supply and tax policy
University lecturers' pay, funding of universities and academic freedom
National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) and campus unions
Students' welfare, fees and sometimes wider public causes
A cause (rights, the environment) rather than members' pockets

blocks.markdown:
### Pressure group distinguished from a political party

The two are often confused because both try to shape what government does. The differences are sharp.

A **party** seeks to win elections and occupy the offices of President, Governor and legislator. A **pressure group** does not put up candidates for those offices (and section 221 of the 1999 Constitution would forbid it from canvassing for votes). A party must have a broad programme covering many issues; a pressure group may care about one issue only. A party is responsible to the whole electorate if it wins; a pressure group is responsible to its members. A party is ready to form and run government; a pressure group is content to remain outside and lobby those who do.

items: **Lobbying** — private meetings with ministers, legislators and officials to argue a case.
**Publicity and the media** — press conferences, adverts, social media campaigns and sponsored documentaries.
**Petitions and peaceful demonstrations** — presenting signatures and assembling where the Constitution's section 40 right of peaceful assembly allows.
**Strikes, work-to-rule and boycotts** — especially by labour and professional groups (NLC, ASUU, NMA).
**Litigation** — taking government to court, a method used frequently by the NBA and civil-liberties groups.
**Expert advice and research** — supplying technical information that ministries lack.
**Electioneering influence** — endorsing or campaigning against candidates without itself standing, and reminding parties of bloc votes.
**Ultimatums and threats of non-cooperation** — for example, doctors withdrawing services until a pay agreement is honoured.

blocks.title: Why some Nigerian groups succeed
blocks.text: Influence depends on membership size, unity, funds, the strategic position of members (doctors and oil workers can halt essential services), the quality of leadership, public sympathy, and whether the group is acting inside the law. A divided union, or one that the public sees as selfish, loses leverage even if it is large.

blocks.title: Classifying the NLC and distinguishing it from the PDP
blocks.prompt: In an examination, a candidate is asked to show that the Nigeria Labour Congress is a pressure group and not a political party. Construct the answer.

steps.text: Define both terms in one sentence each. A pressure group influences policy without seeking to form government; a party contests elections in order to form government.
Identify the NLC. It is the central labour organisation of Nigerian workers, an associational and interest group whose members are wage earners, not a cross-section of the whole electorate.

Apply the tests. The NLC does not register candidates for President or the National Assembly; it does not publish a manifesto covering defence, foreign policy and taxation as a governing programme; it uses strikes, bargaining and publicity rather than the ballot.
Contrast with the PDP. The People's Democratic Party is registered with INEC, contests every general election, has occupied the presidency, and exists to win and exercise power.
Anticipate a trap. The NLC may endorse a candidate or threaten to campaign against a government — that is influence, not an attempt to form government. Endorsement does not turn a union into a party.
Conclude. On every defining test — aim, method, membership and responsibility — the NLC is a pressure group.

blocks.answer: The NLC is an associational interest group of workers that uses strikes, bargaining and publicity to influence policy; it does not contest elections or seek to form government, which is what the PDP, as a registered party, exists to do

blocks.title: Name Nigerian examples, not foreign ones
blocks.text: A definition without an example scores half. Always attach NLC, NMA, NBA, MAN, ASUU or a student union to the type you have named. And never write that a pressure group 'forms government' — that single error turns the answer into a description of a party.

points: A pressure group is an organised association that tries to influence government without seeking to form it.
Interest (sectional) groups defend members' material interests; promotional (cause) groups advance a cause for society at large.
Almond's types — associational, institutional, non-associational and anomic — classify groups by how they are organised.
A party contests elections and seeks power; a pressure group stays outside the contest and lobbies those who hold it.
Nigerian examples include the NLC, NMA, NBA, MAN, ASUU and student unions.
Methods include lobbying, publicity, petitions, strikes, litigation and expert advice. Influence depends on size, unity, funds, strategic position and public support.
